title: Ideal gas equation
examples: How do I use the gas constant R in this equation?
What are the standard units I must use for pressure and volume?
If the temperature changes, how does that affect the gas volume?

explain.say: Today we learn the ideal gas equation. This equation links pressure, volume, moles, and temperature.
Pressure, or P, is the force exerted per unit area. We measure this in atmospheres or pascals.
Volume, or V, tells us the space the gas occupies. We usually measure this in liters or cubic meters.
Moles, or n, represents the amount of substance present. One mole is Avogadro's constant amount.
Temperature, or T, must always be measured in kelvin. Remember to convert from Celsius to kelvin.
The gas constant, R, is a fixed value that connects all these units. Its value depends on the units used.

faq.q: What are the standard units I should use for this equation?
faq.a: You should use standard units like atmospheres for pressure, liters for volume, moles for amount, and kelvin for temperature.
asks: Do I need to convert anything before using R?

faq.q: Does the gas constant R change if I change the units?
faq.a: Yes, the value of R changes depending on the units you choose for pressure and volume.
asks: Is R always the same number?
How do I pick the right value for R?

faq.q: If I use Celsius for temperature, will my answer be wrong?
faq.a: Yes, you must always convert the temperature from degrees Celsius to kelvin before using the equation.
asks: What is the conversion from C to K?

faq.q: What does 'n' represent in this formula?
faq.a: The 'n' represents the number of moles of gas you are dealing with in your calculation.
asks: How do I find the number of moles?

faq.q: Can I rearrange the equation to find pressure?
faq.a: Yes, you can rearrange it to solve for pressure by dividing the other terms by P.
asks: How do I find P if I know everything else?
What is the formula for pressure?

facts: The ideal gas equation is written as P times V equals n times R times T.
Temperature (T) must always be expressed in kelvin for this equation to work correctly.
When using standard units, the gas constant R is often given as 0 point 0821 L atm divided by mol K.
If you change the units, you must change the value of the gas constant R accordingly.

quiz.say: A gas occupies a volume of 10 liters at 27 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere. If the number of moles is 1 point 0 mole, what is the pressure?
quiz.why: You must convert 27 degrees Celsius to kelvin first. Then, rearrange the formula to solve for P using the correct value for R.

wrong.0: This mistake incorrectly uses the gas constant R value without considering the temperature conversion.
wrong.1: This mistake only uses the volume and ignores the pressure and temperature variables.
wrong.3: This mistake forgets to account for the temperature and the gas constant R.

quiz.say: If you keep the pressure and temperature constant, how does the volume of a gas change if you double the moles?
quiz.why: Because volume (V) is directly proportional to moles (n) when P and T are constant, doubling n doubles V.

wrong.0: This mistake ignores the direct relationship between moles and volume described by the law.
wrong.1: This mistake incorrectly assumes a squared relationship between moles and volume.
wrong.2: This mistake confuses the direct relationship with an inverse relationship.

quiz.say: A gas sample has a volume of 5 liters, is at 27 degrees Celsius, and 2 moles. If the pressure is 1 atmosphere, what is the gas constant R?
quiz.why: You must first convert 27 degrees Celsius to 27 plus 273 equals 300 kelvin. Then, rearrange the formula to solve for R.

wrong.0: This mistake forgets the temperature unit entirely when calculating R.
wrong.1: This mistake incorrectly assumes the value of R is simply 1.
wrong.3: This mistake uses the wrong unit for temperature in the gas constant R.
